questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] a zero-downtime schema change on a live product (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/07). The product wants to rename the issue field storyPoints to estimate on a 2.1M-row Issue table that takes about 400 writes/s at peak and can tolerate only about 1 s of blocked writes, and the same release adds an index on that table. Migrations run in a release phase on a throwaway machine before any new instance serves, at least 2 machines stay up through a rolling deploy, and browsers can keep running the previous SPA bundle after the API has moved on. Write your release plan before you look: what compatibility each release must hold, the lock every DDL statement takes, how the data moves across, what stale clients do mid-change, how you prove the old column is dead, and what a rollback looks like at each step. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] First ask whether the database name has to change at all: mapping the renamed model field onto the existing column makes the generated migration empty, so there is no SQL to make safe.
keyPoints.quote: keep the column and map the field with Prisma

keyPoints.text: [w3] The plan is a compatibility matrix (old binary against the new schema, new binary against the old schema) and every cell is green for every release, because a release-phase runner plus two live machines guarantees old code serves against the changed schema.
keyPoints.quote: produce the compatibility matrix (old binary × new schema, new binary × old schema)

keyPoints.text: [w2] Review the SQL the ORM emits, never the model diff: a rename comes out as a drop plus an add, which deletes the data during the release phase.

[w3] Each DDL statement in the plan states the lock it takes and is checked against the ~1 s write-blocking budget; a statement that would block writes for longer than that (a plain index build, a type change that rewrites the table) is redesigned, not scheduled.
keyPoints.quote: every DDL statement lists its lock level

keyPoints.text: [w3] If the column itself has to move, the data crosses over in a multi-release sequence, each step its own deploy: an additive nullable column first; then a release that keeps both columns in step while every read still comes from the original; then a throttled, resumable, idempotent backfill job outside the migration transaction; then reads cut over (behind a flag if possible); then the original column stops being written but stays in place for one more release; only then the drop. Rollback at any step is redeploying the previous binary, which works because no step has yet removed anything that binary still uses.
keyPoints.quote: with each step as its own release

keyPoints.text: [w2] The new index is built online (CONCURRENTLY on Postgres) so writes keep flowing for the whole build; that form refuses to run inside a transaction, so it ships as its own migration that the runner does not wrap in one.
keyPoints.quote: These can't run inside a transaction.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Stale SPA bundles keep PATCHing the old field name; a lenient request schema strips the unknown key and answers 200 while saving nothing, so the plan decides how the API treats the old key until those clients are gone.
[w2] The contract step ships only with evidence: a query that proves nothing reads the old column any more.
keyPoints.quote: the contract step has a query that proves nothing reads

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the change ships and goes wrong: the release-phase migration runs while old machines still serve, the canary looks clean, a rollback is triggered, and CI was green the whole time. Walk the failure windows: what breaks, who notices first, and what in your plan already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A destructive statement in the release phase loses data before any new code runs, and the old machines still selecting the dropped column return 5xx on the issue-list and sprint-report routes until the last old machine is replaced.

[w3] A clean canary proves only the new-binary cell; a rollback runs the previous binary against the already-migrated schema, so the errors can arrive only after rolling back (atlas, for example, saw zero canary errors and then a 40% error rate after the rollback).
[w2] A runner that fails partway must be safe to run again, and it has to finish before any new pod starts serving.
[w3] Green CI is not evidence here: a test database built from scratch has no rows to lose and no old binary running against it, so the mismatch can never show up in tests.
keyPoints.quote: A fresh database has no rows to lose and no old code running against it.

keyPoints.text: [w1] Before relying on an online index build, check on a scratch database how the ORM's runner executes a multi-statement migration file.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your plan against the alternatives the chapter itself names: mapping the field vs a real database rename, a one-shot in-place ALTER vs a multi-release sequence, strict vs lenient request validation during the change, and release-phase migrations vs schema-from-model at startup. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] A model-level mapping needs no SQL at all; a true database rename is only worth it if the column name itself must change, and then it becomes a multi-release project.
keyPoints.quote: if the database name truly must change

keyPoints.text: [w1] The cost of mapping: the naming inconsistency stays in the schema, and a later 'mapping-only' tidy-up PR is a rename in disguise (atlas INC-004).
keyPoints.quote: That inconsistency is exactly what INC-004

keyPoints.text: [w3] A one-shot in-place type change was harmless on an empty early database, but on a live Postgres table a type change such as double precision to text rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.
keyPoints.quote: It was harmless on an empty early-sprint database.

keyPoints.text: [w2] Strict validation turns the silent loss into a loud 400, but it also rejects every client still on the previous bundle during the N-1 window; name which cost you accept.
keyPoints.quote: the one-word Zod change that would have turned the silent loss into a loud 400

keyPoints.text: [w3] Running migrations in a release phase buys one run before new instances serve and an aborted deploy on failure, but it also guarantees the old code meets the new schema, so every schema change must stay backward compatible.
keyPoints.quote: made it worse, because it guaranteed old code would meet the new schema

keyPoints.text: [w2] Schema-from-model at startup (EnsureCreated) looks simpler but never alters an existing database, and a test suite built on it with no migration step in CI (atlas) can never catch a migration that breaks the running binary.
keyPoints.quote: can never see a migration-vs-old-binary mismatch
